title: Alone in the Dark
full_review:
January is to movie studios what November is to supermarkets: a time to unload their turkeys. And while still early, a strong contender for this year's Golden Gobbler is "Alone in the Dark" (Lions Gate), an insufferably inane sci-fi action film which could possibly be one of the worst movies in recent memory.

And don't just take my word for it. During an advance screening, the movie was met with bursts of unintended laughter and when a faulty projector twice interrupted the viewing the audience actually applauded.

Based on a popular violent video game (need I say more?), the incoherent plot involves a paranormal detective, Edward Carnby (Christian Slater), who is investigating the disappearance of 19 people, all of whom grew up in the same orphanage in which he did. Carnby's search leads him to Professor Hudgens (Mathew Walker), an anthropologist obsessed with unlocking the secrets of a highly advanced ancient Indian tribe which was wiped out when they opened a portal to another world and released a race of evil creatures. Hudgens is scouring the globe to find artifacts which, when pieced together, will form a key to reopen the portal. Why? Who knows? Who cares?

As it turns out, the missing orphans had, as children, been test subjects in Hudgens' mutation experiments. Hudgens procured his victims with the help of the Catholic nun who ran the orphanage. Carnby narrowly escaped the same fate, but his memory of the events has since been erased.

Bending suspension of disbelief to the breaking point, Tara Reid plays brainy anthropologist Aline Cedrac, Hudgens' unwitting colleague and Carnby's former flame.

As directed by Uwe Boll, the film's ludicrous script, risible dialogue and bafflingly bad acting makes Ed Wood's campy cult classic, "Plan 9 From Outer Space," look like "Citizen Kane" by comparison.

The odious effect of the movie's pointless and protracted video game-style carnage -- a combination of "Aliens" and "28 Days Later" -- is compounded by its ear-splitting soundtrack.
If you're foolish enough to buy a ticket to this bottom-trawling fare, you may just find yourself sitting alone in the dark.

The film contains excessive gratuitous violence and gore, a suicide, an implied sexual encounter, as well as much rough and crude language and profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
